title: Paid more the year after falling short
question: Which providers fell below the monitor's standard and received more City money the following year?
finding: 37 provider-years fell below the threshold and have payment figures for the following year; in 21 of them the department paid the provider more the next year, $48.4 million more in total. 13 of the 21 were reviews of the two pandemic years. Top of the list by weight of the monitor's finding: 3rd Street Youth Center & Clinic, $509,942 in fiscal year 2022 and $1.0 million the year after (overall score 1).
how: Threshold, stated plainly: for Public Health, at least one programme reviewed that year was given an overall score of 1 or 2 on the monitor's 4-point scale, or met less than 80% of its contracted performance objectives; for homelessness contracts, the department's monitor wrote that not all contract objectives were met or fully reported. Payments are everything that department paid the organization in the fiscal year reviewed, the next year and the year after. City money is taken from the Controller's nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only and leaves out other payments to the same organizations.
limits: A rise in payments after a weak review is not a reward for it. Reviews are completed months after the fiscal year ends, so the following year's budget was usually fixed first; most rises are cost-of-living increases or new programmes unrelated to the one reviewed; and one weak programme among many says little about the rest. In the pandemic years objectives were often missed because sites were closed or clients could not be seen. The useful question is whether the weak programme itself was corrected, which the published papers rarely say.
